pos: n. (the imperial assembly at Worms in 1521 before which Martin Luther refused to recant his writings, and which then outlawed him by the Edict of Worms)
etymology: Diet from Medieval Latin dieta, a day's session, an assembly; Worms is a city on the Rhine.
biblical_def: The Diet of Worms was the first assembly of the young emperor Charles V, and Luther came to it under a safe-conduct in April 1521. On 17 April he was shown a table of his books and asked whether they were his and whether he would recant. He asked for a day. On 18 April he answered that unless he was convinced by the testimony of Scripture or by clear reason, he could not and would not recant, for his conscience was captive to the Word of God, and to go against conscience was neither safe nor right. Early printed accounts add, ‘Here I stand; I can do no other. God help me.’ His stand was the apostles': “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29), and the psalmist's: “I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed” (Psa 119:46). The Edict of Worms in May declared him an outlaw whom any man might kill. Jeremiah's experience was his: “his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones” (Jer 20:9). Christ's promise covered him: “fear not them which kill the body” (Mat 10:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines diet as an assembly of the states or circles of the empire of Germany and of other countries, for the purpose of deliberating on affairs of state.
webster_full: DIET, n. An assembly of the states or circles of the empire of Germany and of Poland; a convention of princes, electors, ecclesiastical dignitaries and representatives of free cities, to deliberate on the affairs of the empire.
2. Food or victuals; a course of food regulated by the rules of medicine.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed.
Jer 20:9

Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
corruption_summary: ‘Here I stand’ has become a slogan of personal authenticity — my truth against the system — when Luther's whole point was that his conscience was bound, not free.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern hero refuses to recant because he will not betray himself. Luther refused because he could not betray the Word. His conscience was captive, not sovereign, and the condition he set was precise: show me from Scripture or from evident reason that I am wrong, and I will be the first to burn my books. That is the opposite of the autonomous conscience that now quotes him. A conscience that answers to nothing but itself is not Luther's; it is the spirit he opposed in the radicals of his own day.

The recovery is a conscience bound to Scripture and therefore free from men. The 1689 Confession states it: God alone is Lord of the conscience, and has left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are contrary to His Word. A man standing alone before an emperor is admirable only if he is standing on the Word.
roots_summary: Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey; Hebrew edah (H5713), testimony; Hebrew ba'ar (H1197), to burn.
roots_lines: Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; Acts 5:29.
usage: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — Luther before the emperor.
“will not be ashamed” (Psa 119:46) — the answer of 18 April 1521.
“as a burning fire shut up in my bones” (Jer 20:9) — why he could not recant.

pos: n. (the Wartburg, the castle above Eisenach in Thuringia where Luther was hidden from May 1521 to March 1522 and translated the New Testament into German)
etymology: German Wartburg, ‘watch-castle,’ from warten, to watch, and Burg, castle.
biblical_def: The Wartburg was where Frederick the Wise had Luther taken after Worms, seized on the road by friendly horsemen in a staged kidnapping so that the elector could deny knowing where he was. For ten months Luther lived there as ‘Junker Jörg,’ Knight George, grew a beard, suffered in body and spirit, and worked. In about eleven weeks he translated the whole New Testament from Erasmus's Greek into German, published in September 1522; the book shaped the German language and put the Scriptures into the hands of ploughmen and housewives. Paul had told Timothy what such a book could do: “the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus” (2Ti 3:15). The work rested on the conviction of the apostolic church that the Word belongs to all: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly” (Col 3:16); “Search the scriptures” (Joh 5:39). When news came that Karlstadt and others at Wittenberg were overturning altars and images by force, Luther left the castle in March 1522 against the elector's wishes and in eight sermons restored order by preaching, trusting that the Word would do what violence could not. As the prophet asked, “Is not my word like as a fire?” (Jer 23:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines translation as the act of turning into another language; interpretation; a version.
webster_full: TRANSLATION, n. The act of removing or conveying from one place to another.
2. The act of turning into another language; interpretation; as the translation of the Scriptures.
3. That which is produced by turning into another language; a version.
scriptures: And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
corruption_summary: The Wartburg is honoured for a translation and forgotten for its sequel: Luther left it to stop a reformation by force, convinced that the Word must do the work.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular history celebrates Luther's German Bible and pays little attention to the eight sermons he preached on his return, in which he told the Wittenberg radicals that he would preach, teach and write, but compel no one by force; that the Word had done everything while he slept and drank beer with his friends. The temptation to reform by coercion, to smash what offends rather than to persuade consciences, recurs in every movement, including Christian political movements now.

The recovery is both halves of the Wartburg: put the Scriptures into the people's tongue, and then trust them. A church that has the Bible in every language and still reaches for pressure and spectacle to change hearts has forgotten what Luther learned in that castle.
roots_summary: Greek graphe (G1124), scripture; sophizo (G4679), to make wise; ereunao (G2045), to search.
usage: “able to make thee wise unto salvation” (2Ti 3:15) — the September Testament of 1522.
“Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly” (Col 3:16) — Scripture for the household.
“Is not my word like as a fire?” (Jer 23:29) — why Luther left the castle to preach.

pos: n. (the public debate at Leipzig in June and July 1519 between Johann Eck and the Wittenberg theologians Karlstadt and Luther, in which Luther denied that popes and councils cannot err)
etymology: Latin disputatio, a formal academic debate, from disputare, to discuss. Held in the Pleissenburg castle before Duke George of Saxony.
biblical_def: The Leipzig Disputation was Johann Eck's attempt to draw Luther into open heresy, and he succeeded in drawing out the principle of the Reformation. Eck, a skilled debater, first engaged Karlstadt on grace and free will, then Luther on the primacy of Rome. Luther argued that the primacy of the pope was of human, not divine, right, and that the Greek church had never been under it. Eck pressed him toward the Hussites, and Luther, studying the records, said that among the articles of Hus condemned at Constance some were thoroughly Christian and evangelical. He went on to say that a council could err. The judges declared no winner, but the line had been crossed: Scripture stood above pope and council. It was the Berean principle: “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11), and Isaiah's test, “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). Paul had shown that even an apostle could be withstood “to the face, because he was to be blamed” (Gal 2:11), and every tradition must answer to the Word: “Why do ye also transgress the commandment of God by your tradition?” (Mat 15:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines disputation as the act of disputing; a reasoning or argumentation in opposition to something; an exercise in colleges, in which parties reason in opposition to each other on some question proposed.
webster_full: DISPUTATION, n. The act of disputing; a reasoning or argumentation in opposition to something, or on opposite sides; controversy in words.
2. An exercise in colleges, in which parties reason in opposition to each other, on some question proposed.
scriptures: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Gal 2:11
But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.
Mat 15:3
But he answered and said unto them, Why do ye also transgress the commandment of God by your tradition?
corruption_summary: At Leipzig Luther said councils can err, and that single admission is still the dividing line between the Reformation and every church that places its tradition beyond correction.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome holds that ecumenical councils, approved by the pope, cannot err in defining doctrine. Eastern Orthodoxy holds the same of its seven councils. Many evangelicals, without saying so, treat their own denominational traditions as practically unreformable. Luther's admission at Leipzig cut through all of it: the church's councils are fallible witnesses, to be honoured where they agree with Scripture and corrected where they do not.

The 1689 Confession says it plainly, that the supreme judge in all controversies of religion, all decrees of councils, opinions of ancient writers and doctrines of men, can be no other than the Holy Scripture delivered by the Spirit. The recovery is to hold that line without contempt for the councils, as Luther did, quoting them where they were right.
roots_summary: Greek anakrino (G350), to search, examine; Hebrew torah (H8451), law, instruction; Greek paradosis (G3862), tradition.
usage: “whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) — the Berean test applied to popes and councils.
“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the standard Luther set above Constance.
“transgress the commandment of God by your tradition” (Mat 15:3) — why a council can err.

pos: n. (Andreas Bodenstein von Karlstadt, 1486–1541, Wittenberg theologian who gave Luther his doctorate, pressed reform by force during Luther's absence in 1521–22, and later broke with him over the Supper)
etymology: From Karlstadt in Franconia, his birthplace; his family name was Bodenstein. Also spelled Carlstadt.
biblical_def: Karlstadt was senior to Luther at Wittenberg and presided at the ceremony that made Luther a doctor of theology in 1512. He was converted to Augustine's doctrine of grace soon after Luther and debated Eck at Leipzig. While Luther was hidden at the Wartburg, Karlstadt took the lead at Wittenberg. On Christmas Day 1521 he celebrated the Supper in ordinary clothes, without the canon of the mass, giving both bread and cup to the people — a right reform, done in haste. He urged the removal of images, and crowds broke them; he married, renounced his academic title, and dressed as a peasant. Luther returned and halted the changes, not because they were wrong in themselves but because they were forced on weak consciences. Paul's rule was his: “Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations” (Rom 14:1), and “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). Karlstadt went on to teach a purely symbolic Supper, quarrelled bitterly with Luther, wandered, and ended his life as a professor at Basel. The conflict illustrates James: “the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (Jas 1:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines zeal as passionate ardour in the pursuit of any thing; eagerness of desire to accomplish or obtain some object.
webster_full: ZEAL, n. Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing.
2. In general, zeal is eagerness of desire to accomplish or obtain some object, and it may be manifested either in favour of any person or thing, or in opposition to it.
scriptures: Rom 14:1
Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Jas 1:20
For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
But if thy brother be grieved with thy meat, now walkest thou not charitably. Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died.
corruption_summary: Karlstadt was often right about what should change and wrong about how, and the reformer who confuses haste with faithfulness is a permanent type in the church.
corruption_paragraphs: Karlstadt's reforms — the cup restored, the mass abolished, images removed — were mostly the reforms the Reformed churches later made. His error was to treat the timetable as a matter of conscience and the weak as obstacles. The same temper appears whenever a church leader, convinced of a true principle, imposes it overnight and calls the resistance unbelief. Zeal without patience wounds those for whom Christ died.

The recovery is the pastoral wisdom Luther showed in 1522 and Paul in Romans 14: change what God commands, but teach before you change, and bear with the weak while you teach. The Reformed regulative principle is not served by mobs breaking windows.
roots_summary: Greek astheneo (G770), to be weak; euschemonos (G2156), decently; orge (G3709), wrath.
roots_lines: Greek astheneo (G770) — to be weak, feeble; Romans 14:1, 21.
usage: “Him that is weak in the faith receive ye” (Rom 14:1) — why Luther halted the Wittenberg changes.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — reform without riot.
“the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (Jas 1:20) — Karlstadt's lesson.

pos: n. (Thomas Müntzer, c. 1489–1525, German radical preacher who appealed to direct revelation by the Spirit against the written Word, led peasant forces at Frankenhausen, and was executed)
etymology: German surname, also spelled Münzer, ‘coiner.’ Luther called him the spirit of Allstedt.
biblical_def: Thomas Müntzer began as a follower of Luther and became his fiercest enemy. He taught that the true Christian must receive the living word of God directly by the Spirit, in dreams and visions and the inner voice, and he mocked the Wittenbergers' trust in the written Scriptures as a dead letter. In his ‘Sermon to the Princes’ at Allstedt in 1524 he urged the Saxon rulers to take the sword and slay the godless, and when they would not, he turned to the people. In the Peasants' War of 1525 he joined the rebels at Frankenhausen under a rainbow banner, promising that he would catch the cannonballs in his sleeves; the princes' army destroyed the peasants, Müntzer was captured, tortured, and beheaded. Scripture had judged his method beforehand: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jn 4:1), for false prophets “speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD” (Jer 23:16). And it had judged his sword: “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52); “Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath” (Rom 12:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fanaticism as excessive enthusiasm; wild and extravagant notions of religion; religious frenzy.
webster_full: FANATICISM, n. Excessive enthusiasm; wild and extravagant notions of religion; religious frenzy.
FANATIC, n. A person affected by excessive enthusiasm, particularly on religious subjects.
scriptures: Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
corruption_summary: Müntzer is now honoured as a social revolutionary; the Reformers saw what modern admirers miss — that his politics followed from setting the Spirit against the Word.
corruption_paragraphs: Marxist historians made Müntzer a hero of the class struggle, and liberation theology has claimed him as a prophet of the poor. The economic grievances of the peasants were real. But Müntzer's revolution grew out of his theology: once the inner voice outranks Scripture, the prophet's vision becomes the law, and the sword of the elect becomes the means of the kingdom. The same pattern reappears in every movement that claims fresh revelation and a mandate to purge the ungodly.

The recovery is the Reformation's double rule. The Spirit speaks in and through the written Word, never against it; and the kingdom of Christ advances by the Word and Spirit, not by insurrection. Luther opposed Müntzer for the first reason and Romans 13 for the second. Both stand.
roots_summary: Greek dokimazo (G1381), to try, test; Hebrew chazown (H2377), vision; Greek machaira (G3162), sword.
usage: “try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jn 4:1) — against the inner word of Allstedt.
“they speak a vision of their own heart” (Jer 23:16) — the source of Müntzer's revelations.
“all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52) — Frankenhausen, 1525.

pos: n. (Conrad Grebel, c. 1498–1526, Zurich humanist and disciple of Zwingli who broke with him over infant baptism and on 21 January 1525 performed the first believer's baptism of the Reformation era)
etymology: Swiss German surname. Leader of the circle later called the Swiss Brethren.
biblical_def: Conrad Grebel was the son of a Zurich patrician, educated at Vienna and Paris, and one of the young men who studied the Greek New Testament with Zwingli. Reading it, they became convinced that baptism belongs to those who believe, and that the church is a gathered company of believers rather than the whole population of a town. Zwingli had once leaned the same way, but drew back when the city council decided for infant baptism. On the evening of 21 January 1525, in the house of Felix Manz's mother, George Blaurock asked Grebel to baptize him, and Grebel did, and Blaurock baptized the others. The pattern they read was Luke's: “they that gladly received his word were baptized” (Act 2:41); Philip's condition, “If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest” (Act 8:37); and Christ's order, “He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved” (Mar 16:16). They understood baptism as Paul did, a burial into Christ's death and rising “in newness of life” (Rom 6:4). Grebel was imprisoned, escaped, and died of plague in 1526; Manz was drowned in the Limmat by the Zurich council in 1527. This dictionary, standing in the 1689 Confession's Particular Baptist line, owns their recovery of believer's baptism, while not owning everything the Swiss Brethren later taught.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines baptism as the application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ceremony, by which he is initiated into the visible church of Christ.
webster_full: BAPTISM, n. The application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ceremony, by which he is initiated into the visible church of Christ.
2. Baptism of the Holy Spirit is the miraculous effusion of the Spirit.
scriptures: Act 2:41
Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
Act 8:37
And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.
He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned.
Rom 6:4
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.
corruption_summary: Grebel's baptism is dismissed by paedobaptist histories as sectarian and claimed by modern individualism as a free choice; it was neither, but obedience to the apostolic order of faith and then baptism.
corruption_paragraphs: Reformed histories written from the territorial churches long treated the Zurich Brethren as fanatics lumped with Münster, and the Zurich council drowned them as rebels. Modern sympathisers make the opposite mistake, presenting them as pioneers of voluntary religion and personal autonomy. Their own reason was Scriptural: they found no infant baptism in the New Testament and found believers baptized throughout it.

The 1689 Confession confesses that those who actually profess repentance toward God, faith in and obedience to the Lord Jesus, are the only proper subjects of this ordinance. The recovery is to honour Grebel's obedience while confessing, with the Particular Baptists, the full Reformed doctrine of grace, the magistrate and the oath which the Swiss Brethren did not hold.
roots_summary: Greek baptizo (G907), to baptize, immerse; pisteuo (G4100), to believe; sunthapto (G4916), to bury with.
roots_lines: Greek baptizo (G907) — to dip, immerse, baptize; Acts 2:41, 8:38, Mark 16:16.
Greek sunthapto (G4916) — to bury together with; Romans 6:4, Colossians 2:12.
usage: “they that gladly received his word were baptized” (Act 2:41) — the order Grebel followed in 1525.
“If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest” (Act 8:37) — the condition of baptism.
“buried with him by baptism into death” (Rom 6:4) — what the ordinance signifies.

pos: n. (Balthasar Hubmaier, c. 1480–1528, Anabaptist theologian, author of On Heretics and Those Who Burn Them, who unlike the Swiss Brethren upheld the Christian magistrate and was burned at Vienna)
etymology: German surname. Doctor of theology under Johann Eck at Ingolstadt before his conversion to the Reformation.
biblical_def: Balthasar Hubmaier was the only trained theologian among the early Anabaptist leaders, a former pupil of Eck and a cathedral preacher at Regensburg. At Waldshut he embraced the Reformation and then believer's baptism, receiving it at Easter 1525. In 1524 he wrote On Heretics and Those Who Burn Them, one of the first pleas of the Reformation era against putting heretics to death. He argued from the parable of the tares, “Let both grow together until the harvest” (Mat 13:30), and from Paul's method of correction, “In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance” (2Ti 2:25). His motto was that truth is immortal. Unlike the Swiss Brethren, Hubmaier taught in On the Sword (1527) that a Christian may serve as a magistrate and that the ruler is “the minister of God to thee for good” (Rom 13:4). In Moravia he led a large congregation at Nikolsburg. Handed over to the Habsburg authorities, he was burned in Vienna on 10 March 1528, and his wife Elsbeth, who had urged him to stand firm, was drowned in the Danube three days later. Christ's saying was fulfilled in them: “he that endureth to the end shall be saved” (Mat 10:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines persecution as the act or practice of persecuting; the infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, for adhering to a religious creed or mode of worship.
webster_full: PERSECUTION, n. The act or practice of persecuting; the infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed or mode of worship.
2. The state of being persecuted.
scriptures: Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.
In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth;
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
And ye shall be hated of all men for my name's sake: but he that endureth to the end shall be saved.
corruption_summary: Hubmaier held together what later movements split apart — believer's baptism, the lawful sword of the magistrate, and the refusal to kill men for their beliefs — and the 1689 Baptists held the same three.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern accounts usually force a choice: either the Reformed state church with its persecuting magistrate, or the Anabaptist withdrawal from the sword altogether. Hubmaier fits neither. He believed the magistrate bears the sword by God's ordinance against evildoers, and that heresy is to be answered by the Word, not the fire. That position, unusual in 1525, became the conviction of the English Particular Baptists and is confessed in the 1689 Confession's chapters on the civil magistrate and liberty of conscience.

The recovery is that combination. The church disciplines with the Word and the keys; the magistrate punishes crimes with the sword; and neither may burn a man for what he believes. Hubmaier died at the hands of men who did not believe the third point, and his wife with him.
roots_summary: Greek praotes (G4236), meekness; antidiatithemai (G475), to oppose oneself; hupomeno (G5278), to endure.
roots_lines: Greek antidiatithemai (G475) — to set oneself in opposition; 2 Timothy 2:25, the only use.
usage: “Let both grow together until the harvest” (Mat 13:30) — Hubmaier's text against burning heretics.
“In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves” (2Ti 2:25) — how error is to be met.
“the minister of God to thee for good” (Rom 13:4) — his defence of the Christian magistrate.

pos: n. (Michael Sattler, c. 1490–1527, former Benedictine prior who drafted the Schleitheim Confession of the Swiss Brethren and was burned at Rottenburg)
etymology: German surname, ‘saddler.’ The Schleitheim articles of 24 February 1527 are named for the village where they were agreed.
biblical_def: Michael Sattler was prior of the Benedictine monastery of St Peter in the Black Forest when the Reformation reached him; he left, married a former Beguine named Margaretha, and joined the Swiss Brethren. At Schleitheim in February 1527 he drafted seven articles that became the founding statement of the movement: believer's baptism; the ban, or church discipline, after Christ's order, “go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone” (Mat 18:15); the breaking of bread among the baptized; separation from the world, “come out from among them, and be ye separate” (2Co 6:17); pastors chosen by the congregation; refusal of the sword to Christians; and refusal of all oaths, after Christ's word, “Swear not at all” (Mat 5:34). A few months later he was arrested, tried at Rottenburg, had his tongue cut and his flesh torn with hot tongs, and was burned on 21 May 1527; Margaretha was drowned. Even his enemies recorded his calm. The Particular Baptists of the 1689 Confession share his first three articles in substance, and part with him on the last two, confessing that a Christian may lawfully hold the magistrate's office and that a lawful oath is part of religious worship.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines oath as a solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
webster_full: OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
2. The appeal to God in an oath implies that the person imprecates his vengeance and renounces his favour if the declaration is false.
scriptures: Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.
Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
Mat 5:34
But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne:
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
corruption_summary: The Schleitheim articles are now claimed as the charter of Christian pacifism and political withdrawal; a Baptist reading honours Sattler's church order and corrects his reading of the sword and the oath from Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern neo-Anabaptist theology treats Schleitheim's articles on the sword and the oath as the purest form of the Sermon on the Mount, and judges every Christian magistrate and soldier by them. But Christ's prohibition of swearing in Matthew 5 rebuked the casuistry that made some oaths binding and others not; it did not forbid the oath God Himself commanded in the law and swore by in the gospel. Paul calls the ruler God's minister bearing the sword (Rom 13:1–4) without telling Christian rulers to resign.

The recovery is to receive what was right at Schleitheim — a believers' church, real discipline, the Supper fenced, pastors chosen by the flock — and to confess with the 1689 Confession that a lawful oath is part of religious worship and that Christians may lawfully accept and execute the office of a magistrate. Sattler's courage under torture is to be honoured without inheriting his errors.
roots_summary: Greek elencho (G1651), to tell one's fault, convict; aphorizo (G873), to separate; omnuo (G3660), to swear.
roots_lines: Greek aphorizo (G873) — to separate, set apart; 2 Corinthians 6:17.
Greek omnuo (G3660) — to swear, take an oath; Matthew 5:34, Hebrews 6:13, 16.
usage: “tell him his fault between thee and him alone” (Mat 18:15) — Schleitheim's article on the ban.
“come out from among them, and be ye separate” (2Co 6:17) — the article on separation.
“Swear not at all” (Mat 5:34) — the text Sattler read too broadly.

pos: n. (Menno Simons, 1496–1561, Frisian priest who left Rome in 1536 and gathered the scattered peaceful Anabaptists of the Netherlands and north Germany; the Mennonites bear his name)
etymology: Frisian personal name; Simons is a patronymic, ‘son of Simon.’ His motto, printed on his books, was 1 Corinthians 3:11.
biblical_def: Menno Simons was a parish priest in Friesland who began to doubt transubstantiation in 1525 and, reading the New Testament, found no infant baptism in it. He stayed in his parish for years, preaching more evangelically and living, he later confessed, without peace. In 1535 a band of Anabaptists, among them his own brother, seized an old monastery near Bolsward in sympathy with Münster and were slaughtered; Menno said their blood fell on his heart, for they had died for error with a courage he lacked for the truth. In January 1536 he renounced Rome, was baptized, and became the shepherd of the peaceful Anabaptists, travelling under a price on his head for twenty-five years. He wrote against Münster's violence and polygamy and taught a disciplined church of believers. Every book bore his text: “For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11). But Menno also taught that Christ's flesh did not come from Mary but was a heavenly flesh formed in her — an error against “the Word was made flesh” (Joh 1:14) and against Christ “made of a woman” (Gal 4:4), which the Reformed answered and his own heirs largely abandoned.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines foundation as the basis of an edifice; that part of a building which lies on the ground; and, figuratively, the basis or ground-work of any thing.
webster_full: FOUNDATION, n. The basis of an edifice; that part of a building which lies on the ground.
2. The basis or ground-work of any thing; that on which any thing stands and is supported.
scriptures: For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
Joh 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
And ye shall be hated of all men for my name's sake: but he that endureth to the end shall be saved.
In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth;
corruption_summary: Menno is remembered as the gentle founder of a peace church; the honest portrait includes his real courage, his rejection of Münster, and his error about the flesh of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Mennonite heritage and modern peace theology celebrate Menno chiefly for nonresistance and simple living. The Reformed reader honours his rejection of Münster's violence and his long faithfulness under persecution, and confesses believer's baptism with him. But his Christology was defective, and it is not a minor point: if Christ's flesh was not taken from Mary, He is not of our race, and cannot be our kinsman Redeemer. The 1689 Confession confesses that the Son took upon Him man's nature, being conceived of the Virgin Mary, of her substance.

The recovery is a whole portrait. Menno's one foundation was the right foundation, and the Christ who is that foundation is the Word made flesh, born of a woman, bone of our bone. Courage and discipline do not compensate for an error about the Person of Christ, and the Baptist churches that confess the 1689 have always said so.
roots_summary: Greek themelios (G2310), foundation; sarx (G4561), flesh; ginomai (G1096), to be made, become.
roots_lines: Greek ginomai ek gunaikos — made of a woman; Galatians 4:4.
usage: “other foundation can no man lay” (1Co 3:11) — the motto on every book Menno wrote.
“the Word was made flesh” (Joh 1:14) — the truth his doctrine of heavenly flesh denied.
“he that endureth to the end shall be saved” (Mat 10:22) — twenty-five years under a price on his head.

pos: n. (the seizure of the Westphalian city of Münster in 1534–35 by apocalyptic Anabaptists under Jan Matthys and Jan van Leiden, who proclaimed it the New Jerusalem)
etymology: Münster, from Latin monasterium, monastery. The cages in which the leaders' bodies were displayed still hang from the tower of St Lambert's church.
biblical_def: The Münster Rebellion began when the Lutheran preacher Bernhard Rothmann and the town's evangelicals were joined in 1534 by followers of the Dutch prophet Jan Matthys, who declared Münster the New Jerusalem to which the elect must gather before the end. Catholics and Lutherans who would not be rebaptized were driven out; goods were held in common; images and books other than the Bible were destroyed. Matthys, believing himself invincible, rode out against the besieging army of the prince-bishop on Easter 1535 with a few men and was killed. Jan van Leiden succeeded him, had himself crowned king of the New Zion, and, appealing to the patriarchs, introduced polygamy. The city fell in June 1535; the leaders were tortured and executed in January 1536. Christ had foretold such men: “there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders” (Mat 24:24), and Jeremiah exposed their source, “they speak a vision of their own heart” (Jer 23:16). Paul had warned of their end: “they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation” (Rom 13:2). For a century every opponent of believer's baptism threw Münster in its defenders' faces.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rebellion as an open and avowed renunciation of the authority of the government to which one owes allegiance; or the taking of arms traitorously to resist the authority of lawful government.
webster_full: REBELLION, n. An open and avowed renunciation of the authority of the government to which one owes allegiance; or the taking of arms traitorously to resist the authority of lawful government.
2. Open resistance to lawful authority.
scriptures: For there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect.
Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.
Rom 13:2
Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.

But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction.
corruption_summary: Münster was used for a century to smear every believer's baptism; the Particular Baptists answered by confessing the magistrate, the moral law and the Scriptures alone, and by refusing the name Anabaptist.
corruption_paragraphs: The opponents of the English Baptists in the seventeenth century routinely called them Anabaptists and warned that they would turn London into Münster. The 1644 London Confession was written in part to answer that slander, its title page speaking of churches commonly, though falsely, called Anabaptists; the 1689 Confession continued the answer by adopting the Westminster doctrine of the civil magistrate almost word for word. The charge still appears in polemics against credobaptism.

The real lesson of Münster is not about baptism but about revelation and eschatology. When prophets claim new words from God and a date for the end, the Scriptures are set aside and anything becomes possible, polygamy and massacre included. The recovery is the closed canon, the sufficiency of Scripture, and the patience that waits for Christ's kingdom rather than proclaiming it with the sword.
roots_summary: Greek pseudochristos (G5580), false Christ; antitasso (G498), to resist; hairesis (G139), heresy, faction.
roots_lines: Greek pseudochristos (G5580) — a false Messiah; Matthew 24:24, Mark 13:22.
usage: “there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets” (Mat 24:24) — the New Zion of 1534.
“they speak a vision of their own heart” (Jer 23:16) — the source of Münster's prophecies.
“who privily shall bring in damnable heresies” (2Pe 2:1) — how it ended.
